newsitem.title: UK: Markets scent conspiracy to pave way for EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Markets scent conspiracy to pave way for EMU delay.

text.p: Amid a chorus of official assurances that European monetary union will proceed as planned, some voices are singing off key -- and those are the ones the financial markets are listening to.

The lira and Italian bonds plunged on Friday when Italy's prime minister said Germany might request EMU be postponed, and traders and analysts are increasingly suspicious of a conspiracy to soften them up for an eventual announcement of delay.
"I agree with the view that it's a dress rehearsal for the true event," said Giovanna Mossetti at Caboto in Milan.

"What we saw on Friday shows there is a need for gradual movement, because the psychology of traders is not really linear in the way it responds to information," Mossetti, who is a senior economist at Caboto, said on Tuesday.

The EU financial elite has rolled out its big guns to shoot down market talk of EMU delay. The heads of the German and Dutch central banks and European Monetary Institute all insist currency union is on track, while Yves-Thibault de Silguy, the European commissioner for monetary affairs, was quoted on Tuesday as saying postponement could mean the death of EMU.
But Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he was not sure EMU would begin on time in 1999, and said Germany was unlikely to meet the deficit goal required for participation.

The Bundesbank's insistence that the criteria be obeyed to the letter sits awkwardly with doubts that EMU-lynchpin Germany can cut its deficit to three percent of GDPas required under the EMU treaty, analysts said.

"They're not saying Germany might ask for a delay, but if they're saying you've got to have the three percent and we're almost sure Germany won't make it, it's tantamount to saying delay is very likely," said Caboto's Mossetti.

In light of that, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's suggestion that Germany could possibly request EMU delay -- though he swiftly "clarified" that by saying there was no assumption the timetable would be put back -- was no accident, analysts say.

"I don't think it was a slip of the tongue...it's a fact that Germany would find it difficult to hit the three percent nearly as much as other countries will," said Giorgio Radaelli, senior international economist at Lehman Brothers in London.

The market increasingly suspects officials of trying to deflate its EMU expectations, by making shocking remarks and then retracting or clarifying them, so as to soften the eventual blow of a delay announcement, analysts said.

"I think it's a deliberate attempt to manage market expectations on EMU in a fairly gentle manner, rather than coming out one day and saying 'it's all off, chaps' and just watching the market collapse -- because that is what would happen," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC here.

Some note, however, that French markets have barely budged amid the rumours, in contrast to the "peripheral" lira, peseta and Swedish crown. That implies the market is not betting on a generalised postponement of monetary union, they say.

Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC James Capel, said delay would badly hurt countries like Italy and Spain. But official hints now would let markets discount the possibility and make the reality -- if it materialised -- less painful.
"Apart from anything else, (postponement) would hit the peripheral markets particularly hard and would mean they would be less eligible to make it into the first wave," Prior said.
"It could be a cunning ploy to exclude them." REUTER
